title: Surprise! These Stick Insects Were Hiding in Plain Sight
summary:
Imagine an insect that looks like a twig. Scientists in Australia have just found two stick insect species that nobody had named before.

A team at the University of Sydney took a fresh look at a group of stick insects called Anchiale. One of the new species, Anchiale mabiensis, lives in Queensland's Mabi rainforest. Its eggs have a special lid-like part. Scientists have never recorded this in any stick insect or its closest relatives.

The team also fixed an old mix-up. One large stick insect that scientists and insect fans knew well had been identified wrongly for decades. It now has its own name: Anchiale robusta.

Here is the surprising part. Insects once sorted into just two species turned out to be five species. They live from northern New South Wales, along the Queensland coast, and into tropical northern Australia.

People already knew these insects well. More than 1,000 citizen science observations have been submitted to iNaturalist and the Atlas of Living Australia. Even so, new species were still hiding.

"Taxonomy is often a bit like detective work," said lead author Dr. Braxton Jones. He means that sorting out which species is which takes careful searching for clues.

Why does it matter? One of these stick insects sometimes reaches plague-like numbers and strips leaves from trees. It turned out to be more than one species. Telling them apart could help people understand and manage its effects on forests and farms. Scientists also think one more new species may live in Cape York, but they need more specimens to be sure.
why_it_matters: It shows that even animals people already know well can hide new surprises, and that sorting them correctly can help people care for forests and farms.
